meta.title: Who really said "Have no fear of perfection - you'll never reach it"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Salvador Dalí really wrote this — in Diary of a Genius (1964) — but the famous English wording is a smoothed paraphrase of the documented line.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Have no fear of perfection - you'll never reach it'?
meta.ogDescription: Dalí really wrote it, in Diary of a Genius (1964). The popular English wording is a smoothed paraphrase of the documented translation.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: The thought is genuinely Dalí’s: it appears in his Diary of a Genius (1964), which Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ records at p. 44 as “Don’t be afraid of perfection. You will never attain it!” The famous “Have no fear of perfection — you’ll never reach it” is a smoother English paraphrase of that documented line rather than the exact translated wording, so we mark it attributed rather than verified.

source.excerpt: Don’t be afraid of perfection. You will never attain it!
trail: Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ ties the line to Dalí’s Diary of a Genius (1964), p. 44.
There it reads “Don’t be afraid of perfection. You will never attain it!” — the popular “never reach it” is a paraphrase of that translation.
A fuller rendering aimed at painters is catalogued by LibQuotes ↗, cited to a Taschen compilation.
Popular quote sites such as Goodreads ↗ reproduce the smoothed wording with no source cited.
source.excerptNote: In fuller renderings Dalí addresses the line to painters — a compilation in Taschen’s Dalí: The Paintings gives it as “Painters, do not fear perfection. You will never achieve it!” The pocket-sized “Have no fear of perfection — you’ll never reach it” is the smoothed popular form.
source.rightsHolder: Fundació Gala-Salvador Dalí (Dalí estate) and the publishers/translator of Diary of a Genius
source.rightsNote: Diary of a Genius was first published in 1964, with the English translation following in 1965 — both well after 1931, so the text and its translation remain under copyright. Rights rest with the Dalí estate and the book’s publishers and translator.

author.name: Salvador Dalí
author.heading: About Salvador Dalí
author.bio: Salvador Dalí was the flamboyant Spanish Surrealist behind melting clocks and a waxed moustache, as famous for his self-mythologising showmanship as for his painting. Alongside his canvases he produced a torrent of writing — manifestos, memoirs and the aphoristic Diary of a Genius (1964) — where quotable lines like this one first appeared.

misattribution.heading: The catch is the wording, not the author
misattribution.intro: This one isn’t pinned on the wrong person — the drift is in the words. Dalí really wrote it; the internet just smoothed it.

items.why: The circulated “Have no fear of perfection — you’ll never reach it” is not the exact translated line. Documented English editions read “Don’t be afraid of perfection. You will never attain it!” per Wikiquote ↗.
Sites like Goodreads ↗ carry the line with no book or page — and Goodreads itself flags that its quotes are community-added and unverified.

misattribution.truthLine: The idea and the joke are authentically Dalí, from Diary of a Genius (1964); the famous English wording is a later paraphrase of the documented translation, per Wikiquote ↗.

context.heading: Why it stuck
lead: Coming from a man who spent decades performing his own genius — the waxed moustache, the melting clocks, the staged eccentricity — the line reads as self-aware wit: a perfectionist’s permission slip. Its home, Diary of a Genius, is exactly the sort of aphorism-stuffed memoir in which Dalí buffed such one-liners to a shine.
context.pull: A perfectionist’s permission slip, from the century’s great self-mythologiser.
